Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press. Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine , marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war. The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action. After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver. "Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls," Bisleri said, adding it will cooperate with the regulators. The eponymous brand Bisleri, introduced in India in 1965, is a household name in the country where poor water quality often prompts people and tourists to buy packaged water both for homes and at restaurants.A second government source said the batches linked to the unsafe sample had been recalled, and subsequent testing of products showed no issues with water quality.The sample, collected from Bisleri's premises, did not meet prescribed limits on bromate, a chemical formed as a by-product of certain disinfection processes, the FSSAI said in a social media post on Sunday.After Bisleri appealed the finding, the government regulator still found the sample unsafe but instead said it had detected polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs, the FSSAI said.PAHs are of serious public health concern due to their toxic, mutagenic, and carcinogenic properties, according to research published last year on the National Library of Medicine's PubMed database. clusters.text: After winning a thrilling Formula 1 race in Las Vegas, Max Verstappen had some scores to settle off track. The Red Bull driver clashed with Mercedes rival George Russell throughout the weekend as they overtook each other about a dozen times for the lead and traded barbs in the press. Verstappen had the the last laugh — literally. He won the race, while Russell fell to ninth after hitting the barrier on the penultimate lap. “Ha ha, well done! My God,” Verstappen chuckled over team radio after seemingly catching Russell go off in his rearview mirror. It began during Friday’s third practice session, when Russell was preparing for a fast lap and Verstappen blasted past him. Russell forced his way back ahead as the two banged wheels. After that session, Russell tore into Verstappen for a move he deemed unnecessary, portraying him as an arrogant bully. “When you do this, you are screwing this person over. And he does this week in, week out with many drivers. And everybody accepts it. And I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else,” Russell told Sky Sports F1. “So somebody’s got to stand up to that guy.” In Saturday night’s race, Verstappen started first and held the lead, with Russell tucking into second place behind him. Russell repeatedly passed Verstappen, who kept taking back the lead. Their wheel-to-wheel fight grew feistier with defensive moves and a game of strategic battery deployment. On Lap 49 of 50, Russell was running third when he tried to pass Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli for second place on Turn 5, heading into the Sphere section of the track. He locked up and hit the wall, dropping positions as he reversed out. Verstappen disparaged Russell as an unworthy rival when asked if it felt good to defeat the Briton. “He speaks a lot next to the track. clusters.text: A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement. In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.” Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5. “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.” So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . clusters.text: The familiar domain of the planets gives way to a frozen abyss – a vast chasm of space so far from the warmth and light of the Sun that we have barely begun to catalog its contents. The conventional view of trans-Neptunian space is one dominated by a vast belt of small, icy objects, more or less following an orderly march around the Sun. But some of those less orderly orbits may betray the presence of something much larger: a hidden super-Earth out beyond the Kuiper Belt. No, not Planet Nine. A second one. A mysterious world astronomers are calling Planet X2. "It's a bit like the footprints in the snow," planetary scientist Jonti Horner of the University of Southern Queensland in Australia told ScienceAlert. "It's telling you that somebody's been there that you didn't expect." Much of what we know about the Solar System relies on the light of the Sun, which illuminates the objects herein. However, by Neptune's distance – an average of 30.1 astronomical units, or 30 times the distance between Earth and the Sun – that sunlight has become 900 times weaker than the light that reaches Earth. And only a tiny fraction of the light reflected off objects at that distance makes it all the way back to our telescopes. But those telescopes have grown more powerful and sensitive over the decades; and, in recent years, enough objects have been identified in the outer Solar System to begin mapping their orbital distributions. And it's here that questions have arisen – because, while most of the behavior of the outer Solar System can be attributed to the gravitational influence of the known giant planets, particularly Neptune, some niggling, persistent signals are more challenging to explain. clusters.text: A stock selloff driven by doubts about the economic growth potential of artificial intelligence infected commodities, too, dragging crude oil prices down today despite continued tanker attacks in the Persian Gulf. At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $92.55 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $83.45 per barrel. Both were down from the opening of trade in Asia, but they were both higher than their Friday close, suggesting the effect of the stock selloff was limited in energy commodities. The selloff was triggered by developments in the tech sector, with investors questioning the prospects of the AI industry, whose growth is being fuelled by tens of billions in borrowed funds, as noted by Reuters. These doubts apparently flourished last week around Anthropic’s IPO, causing a 10% drop in Nasdaq—the sharpest drop since the pandemic lockdowns. Tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz have become a daily occurrence, based on reports from official Iranian and international sources, with incidents both in the strait itself and outside it, off the coast of Oman. Meanwhile, the Yemeni Houthis continue to strike targets in Saudi Arabia. The latest, according to the Houthis themselves, was a refinery on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast. Meanwhile, the COP31 gathering failed to result in a deal on global emission reduction efforts as countries could not agree on whether the world should phase out oil and gas, and who will pay for it all. This is the first time the Conference of the Parties has failed to end in a deal since 2009. Oil prices have been on a losing streak for three weeks now, largely on reports about supply catching up to demand and even exceeding it, despite the flow of incident reports from the Persian Gulf. Interestingly, not everyone agrees the glut is here, with the IEA expecting it in the current quarter, while OPEC focuses on a demand rebound. By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

clusters.title: Black hole inside a black hole? New study explores bizarre 5D 'Black Saturn'
clusters.snippet: A new mathematical model described a ring-shaped black hole surrounding a smaller one, with both objects capable of rotating in two independent directions in five-dimensional spacetime.
clusters.text: Black holes are generally imagined as massive, spherical objects with gravity so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape them. What if a black hole could take the shape of a giant ring, with another black hole sitting inside it? This structure, called a 'Black Saturn', is a theoretical possibility under Einstein's theory of general relativity when an extra dimension of space is added.A new study has now expanded the theoretical model, showing how the two black holes could rotate independently in two different planes. The research, titled Doubly-spinning Black Saturns, was published on arXiv on November 16 by physicist Jay Armas.It presents a mathematical solution describing a spherical black hole surrounded by a ring-shaped black hole in five-dimensional spacetime. The model also explores how both objects could reach an extreme state while retaining their separate event horizons.What exactly is a Black Saturn?A Black Saturn is a theoretical arrangement involving two black holes of different shapes. At its centre is a spherical black hole, while a much larger, ring-shaped black hole surrounds it.Both objects have their own event horizons. These are boundaries beyond which nothing, including light, can escape the gravitational pull of a black hole.How does this bizarre cosmic structure work?This arrangement is possible in the mathematics of five-dimensional spacetime. Our observable Universe has three dimensions of space and one dimension of time. Adding another spatial dimension allows Einstein's equations to accommodate geometries that are not possible in the familiar four-dimensional setting.As a result, black holes in five-dimensional spacetime do not necessarily have to follow the spherical shape commonly associated with them.How does the new model change the earlier understanding?The original Black Saturn model was proposed in 2007, but it allowed both the central black hole and the surrounding ring to spin in just one plane.In five-dimensional spacetime, objects can rotate in two independent planes. Accounting for both forms of rotation make the mathematical equations more complicated, but it also allows researchers to explore a wider range of possibilities.Armas's latest work removes the earlier restriction. The rise of Thierno Barry may have surprised even the man himself but stands as a fitting reward for single-minded perseverance and the refusal to quit. “Fabulous” was David Moyes’s take on Barry’s last performance for Everton, when a double against Coventry took the striker to 10 goals for the season in all competitions and his team temporarily up to fifth. It was high praise indeed from a manager who does not dispense tributes freely, and can appear to be on the French forward’s case constantly, but was no more than Barry deserved for a display that also featured an assist for Everton’s third goal of the night. His six Premier League goals leave him joint third alongside Evanilson of Bournemouth and Aston Villa’s Nicolas Jackson. “Haaland must be worried about him catching him now,” Moyes said. That line was delivered in jest but also represented a welcome departure from the position Barry found himself in this summer, and from where Everton stood at the close of transfer deadline day. “I’m stopping, I’m stopping,” says Barry in a searingly honest video released on his YouTube channel in September. Entitled Never Give Up, the episode shows the striker doing exactly that after one miss too many during a private training session with his personal coach. He then breaks down in tears, head in hands in despair, after a dressing down from his lawyer. “Don’t give up, bro,” snaps the lawyer. “Where you come from, you can’t give up.” Many players in that position would have buried the footage, afraid of broadcasting weakness or of the vicious comments that would invariably follow on social media. Barry told the BBC he spent three weeks worrying whether to post before deciding: “No, I just need to show myself. They need to learn about me because last season I showed a version of me that is not me. And they need to learn about me, how I train hard to be the best on the pitch.” Barry’s openness was refreshingly well received, even online. clusters.text: Minutes before Anthropic, the maker of Claude, began trading on Nasdaq on November 19, its co-founder and president Daniela Amodei opened her short speech by calling it an “unusual” company, one many even call “weird”. Founded in May 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees who left over what they saw as a culture that did not put AI safety and alignment first, Anthropic is registered as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), a structure that legally binds the company to weigh public benefit alongside profit. Its CEO Dario Amodei has consistently warned about the existential risks of misaligned AI models and pushed for regulation and a slowdown in the race to build frontier models. Rivals and some critics, however, have called this posturing. The provocatively titled “MisAnthropic Statement”, released on the eve of the IPO and signed by a few prominent figures from different fields, said Anthropic was not a safe AI company and urged rejection of its “reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good”. The charts and timeline below trace the unconventional journey of a company seen as a harbinger of everything unusual unfolding in the AI zeitgeist. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion despite listing during a market slump — with many beginning to wonder whether the ballooning investments in AI were a bubble — and against the backdrop of the Republican rout in the U.S. midterms and the Nvidia scandal. It broke the record for the largest-ever IPO, set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX just five months earlier in a more bullish market.

clusters.text: President Donald Trump wants to cap credit card interest rates, pointing to the proposal as one area where he could work with incoming Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill. It's not the first time President Trump has backed the idea, but his campaign promise has gotten little traction so far in the Republican-led Congress. That could change when Democrats take charge of the House and Senate in January following sweeping midterm election gains. “I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America." "I know some people would say that's not free enterprise, but what's free enterprise when you're sitting home, and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue, and they said, 'let's charge a fee that's too high.' So, I'm all for that." Those calls were quickly echoed by Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is poised to chair the Senate committee that oversees banking next year. "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money," Warren wrote on social media on Saturday. Senators Bernie Sanders (I-Vt) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo) previously introduced legislation to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, in line with the president's pitch. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, and Americans are carrying more credit card debt than ever, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve. In a joint statement earlier this year, several groups representing the banking industry opposed proposed caps. “We share the President’s goal of helping Americans access more affordable credit. At the same time, evidence shows that a 10% interest rate cap would reduce credit availability and be devastating for millions of American families and small businesses who rely on and value their credit cards, the very consumers this proposal intends to help," the statement said. A report published by Vanderbilt University last year looked into the potential impact of the policy and found that a 10% cap would save Americans roughly $100 billion a year in credit card interest costs. clusters.text: A former district judge in Prayagraj has alleged that three people cheated him of ₹29.80 lakh in a fraudulent land deal. According to the complaint, former district judge Raghvendra Dutt Mishra, a resident of Mehdauri Colony in Teliarganj, was approached in December 2022 by Ajay Kumar Singh of Sadulpur Kahli and Rakesh Kumar Patel of Fazilabad, both under Bahariya police station jurisdiction. The accused allegedly offered to arrange the purchase of agricultural land belonging to Rakesh’s relatives, Shivpal and Bhagotideen, in Tikri village. They showed Mishra approximately one bigha and 11 biswas of land belonging to one relative and another parcel belonging to Shivpal in Bhadri, assuring him that the transaction could be completed. FCRF Launches Certified Chief Risk Officer (CRO) Program for India’s Risk Leaders The complainant alleged that the accused demanded advance payments to finalise the proposed land transaction. Mishra transferred ₹5 lakh through RTGS on December 18, 2022, followed by two additional transfers of ₹5 lakh each on January 14, 2023. He also allegedly paid ₹9.80 lakh in cash on January 13, 2023. The payments mentioned in the complaint totalled ₹29.80 lakh. Despite receiving the money, the accused allegedly failed to complete the promised transaction and subsequently stopped communicating with him. According to Mishra, a notarised agreement was executed on August 3, 2023, on behalf of Rakesh Kumar Patel and his mother, Vimla Devi. Around the same period, Mishra’s father became seriously ill and subsequently died, delaying his efforts to pursue the transaction. After completing the funeral-related ceremonies, Mishra attempted to contact the accused but allegedly found Rakesh’s mobile phone switched off. When he visited the village, Bhagoti Prasad reportedly refused to recognise Rakesh. Mishra also alleged that the Aadhaar cards and other documents provided during the transaction were forged. The complaint further alleged that Ajay Kumar Singh, his wife Manju Devi and their associates collected money from prospective land buyers before disappearing. Mishra approached the authorities seeking action over the alleged cheating and document forgery. Following directions from the Police Commissioner, Bahariya police registered an FIR against three individuals under provisions relating to cheating, forgery and other offences. clusters.title: GST ITC Denied as Fabricated Transport Documents Failed to Prove Goods Receipt: GSTAT Prayagraj
clusters.text: For professionals and businesses who follow tax, GST and corporate law through the week. For readers who mainly want TaxGuru without ads, plus the judgments and orders. Summary : The GST Appellate Tribunal, State Bench Prayagraj, considered the eligibility of input tax credit (ITC) claimed by M/s Fatehpur Foundry & Engineering Works on two purchases of scrap iron from M/s Ganesh Enterprises during June 2018. The dispute concerned ITC of ₹1,40,827.50 and an aggregate demand of ₹4,16,849.40, including interest and an equivalent penalty under Section 74 of the CGST/SGST Act, 2017. The supplier was found non-existent during a departmental inspection conducted in 2022, nearly four years after the disputed transactions. The appellant contended that the supplier had been registered when the purchases occurred and that its registration had subsequently been cancelled in November 2020. It relied on tax invoices, e-way bills , banking transactions, GSTR-2A entries and the supplier’s returns to establish the genuineness of the purchases. The Tribunal examined whether the goods had actually moved from Kanpur to Fatehpur and whether the appellant had satisfied Section 16(2)(b) . Although the appellant produced goods receipts issued by Ajanta Carriers and weighment slips from Natraaj Electronic Dharmkanta, these documents were submitted for the first time before the Tribunal without following the prescribed procedure for additional evidence. On scrutiny, the Tribunal identified material discrepancies in the goods receipts, including inconsistent consignee and consignor copies, apparent alteration of a receipt number, erased entries, missing vehicle particulars and blank owner and driver details. It considered the transport documents fabricated and held that the weighment slips could not independently establish genuine movement and receipt of goods. The Tribunal acknowledged that the supplier had filed GST returns, disclosed the transactions and discharged tax liability. However, it distinguished the judicial precedents relied upon by the appellant because the central issue was not merely subsequent cancellation of registration or non-payment of tax by the supplier. Rather, the Tribunal found that the supporting transport evidence was unreliable and that the actual receipt of goods had not been established. clusters.title: Two held with firearm, cartridges in Chatra
clusters.text: Hazaribag: Police arrested two men and seized an illegal firearm, three cartridges and a motorcycle in Kunda police station area of Chatra district on Sunday.Acting on information from SP Animesh Naithany, a team led by Simaria SDPO Shubham Nagar Goje Bhau Saheb began checks near Rantha Mor on Kunda-Lawalong road. The men allegedly tried to flee but were caught.Police identified them as Baldev Ganjhu alias Chhotu Ganjhu of Banasam village and Surendra Kumar of Bajrahi village, both in their thirties. A country-made 9mm sixer and one cartridge were found with Baldev, while Surendra, who faces an Arms Act case, had two cartridges. Police also seized a motorcycle.
